question: How directly can historical color forms in -cameke/-came be related to modern Rarámuri color constructions segmented as root + -ka + -me?

historical_morphology.source: Merrill et al. 2020 edition and analysis of Steffel

general_participial_chain.analysis: participial -(a)me with a final -kV/-ke element in Merrill's analysis of complex chains
general_participial_chain.steffel_metacomment: Steffel reports that speakers commonly omitted the final ke in pronunciation and said me or at most mek.

color_pairs.note: Merrill explicitly treats the missing final -ke as evidence of optional use/truncation of the final element.

modern_morphology.source: Compendio básico de la gramática ralámuli, 1997

forms.regions: Baja/Baja-TB and related variants; chó-ka-mi in other regions

independent_modern_grammar.finding: Choguita Rarámuri has a participial suffix -ame; surface -ami can arise through posttonic front-vowel raising in relevant forms.

formal_bridge.assessment: After the independently documented historical omission of final -ke, the historical truncated string and modern segmented form are effectively segmentally identical apart from transcription conventions.
The same direct historical-to-modern bridge is independently present in the white-color family.

what_is_demonstrated: Historical color words in at least black and white occur both with final -ke and without it.
Steffel independently reports general optional omission/truncation of final -ke in participial -ameke forms.
Modern multivariety analysis explicitly segments the corresponding black and white forms as color root + -ka + participial -me/-mi.
Modern -ame is independently identified as participial by Caballero.
what_is_not_demonstrated: That every historical -ameke word had the same internal segmentation as modern forms.
That historical -c/-k before ameke was synchronically the same color morpheme -ka in every relevant eighteenth-century form.

That plural context caused or conditioned historical -ke omission; the attested color truncations happen to occur in plural contexts, but Steffel describes omission as a general pronunciation pattern.

assessment.interpretation: The color evidence provides a direct surface bridge from historical -kameke~-kame to modern -ka-me in two independent roots. This is stronger than a generic resemblance claim and justifies treating color morphology as the clearest internal demonstration of continuity in the project.

next_steps: Test whether red historical forms have an independently attested -came truncation or another route to modern -ka-me.
Determine whether historical -c/-k preceding -(a)meke can be independently identified as the ancestor/equivalent of modern color -ka.
Separate the color-specific bridge from non-color -ameke families in the global diachronic model.
